insight.title: Twelve-Factor processes: disposable compute, durable state elsewhere
insight.one_liner: A twelve-factor process is stateless and share-nothing: persistent correctness state belongs in backing services, while local memory or disk is only disposable working cache.
insight.why_this_matters: 'Stateless' is easy to misunderstand as 'the application has no state.' The useful boundary is narrower: process instances must be disposable because the next request/job may run elsewhere, so anything that must survive belongs outside the process. That same separation remains useful even for modern long-running work, provided durable orchestration state also lives outside disposable compute.

whole_source_map.problem: Scaling, restart, deploy or relocation means a future request/job cannot rely on hidden state inside the process instance that handled earlier work.
whole_source_map.thesis: Keep processes stateless/share-nothing, store persistent data in stateful backing services, and use process-local memory/files only as short-lived disposable cache whose loss does not break correctness.

derived_model.problem: Process-local state couples correctness to one machine/process lifetime and breaks when work is rescheduled or the process restarts.
derived_model.mechanism: Move durable state to backing services; let process memory/files hold only transient working data; route future requests/jobs to any available process without requiring affinity to previous local state.
derived_model.result: Compute instances become replaceable and horizontally scalable, while state durability becomes an explicit responsibility of backing services rather than hidden process lifetime.

central_chain: A process instance cannot be assumed to receive the next request or survive the next deploy/restart.
Therefore data required by future work cannot live only in that process's memory or local filesystem.
Persistent data is moved to a stateful backing service while local storage remains disposable cache for the current work unit.
Session affinity that depends on one process retaining user state defeats this disposability and is rejected.
The factor makes compute disposable; it does not make the whole application stateless or define how every backing service achieves durability.
open_gaps: The source predates durable workflow runtimes and does not define their orchestration-state model.
Backing-service consistency, availability and latency trade-offs are external to this factor.

dominant.title: The process can disappear; the state must not

nodes.label: 01 · Handle
nodes.title: Disposable process
nodes.text: A process handles the current request or job without assuming future affinity.

nodes.label: 02 · Cache
nodes.title: Temporary local work
nodes.text: Memory or local files may hold short-lived data that can be discarded or recomputed.

nodes.label: 03 · Persist
nodes.title: Backing service
nodes.text: Anything needed by future work is written to a durable stateful service.

nodes.label: 04 · Replace
nodes.title: Any next process
nodes.text: A different or restarted process can continue future requests because correctness did not depend on the old local state.

image.reason: The value is the lifetime boundary between disposable process-local work and persistent backing-service state; a sequence is sufficient.

concepts.name: Stateless process
concepts.why_needed: The runtime unit must not require hidden state from an earlier request/job in the same process.

concepts.name: Backing-service state
concepts.why_needed: Persistent application state remains necessary; it is deliberately externalized from disposable compute.

concepts.name: Ephemeral process state
concepts.why_needed: Local memory/files are still useful when their loss is safe and they serve only as temporary working cache.

examples.scenario: A user request lands on a different process than the previous request.
examples.question: Does the session survive because it lives in a backing store, or did the application silently depend on sticky routing and process memory?

examples.scenario: A worker downloads a large file, transforms it and writes the result.
examples.question: Can the local file disappear after the work unit because the durable result has already been persisted elsewhere?

examples.scenario: A worker process is restarted while a multi-day business workflow is waiting.
examples.question: Is durable workflow progress outside the disposable worker, or was process-local memory accidentally treated as orchestration state?

limitations: Stateless processes do not imply a stateless application; the factor explicitly relies on stateful backing services.
Externalizing state introduces network, consistency and backing-service failure modes that this source does not solve.
The factor does not define durable workflow execution; modern workflow state can remain external while workers themselves stay disposable.
Process-local storage is not forbidden when used as disposable cache or temporary working data whose loss does not violate correctness.

use_now: For each service or worker, list the data whose loss on restart would break correctness; anything on that list should not exist only in process memory/local disk.
Distinguish disposable cache from durable state instead of banning local state categorically.
try: Restart or replace one service instance mid-flow and verify that later requests/jobs can continue without session affinity or hidden local files.
build: A small two-instance demo where requests alternate between processes while shared session/work state remains in an external store.
watch: Where externalizing high-volume intermediate state adds unnecessary latency and should remain recomputable local cache instead.
ignore_for_now: Equating generic twelve-factor processes with Temporal-specific Worker, Workflow or Activity concepts.

connections: durable-execution: compatible boundary but different mechanism — durable workflow progress can live outside disposable processes, while this source only defines process statelessness
worker-process: the shared word 'process' does not make Twelve-Factor processes equivalent to Temporal Worker Processes

concepts.label: Stateless process
concepts.summary: A disposable runtime process whose correctness does not depend on state retained from earlier requests or jobs in its own memory or local filesystem.

concepts.label: Backing-service state
concepts.summary: Persistent application data stored outside disposable processes in a stateful service so future requests or jobs can access it regardless of process lifetime.

concepts.label: Ephemeral process state
concepts.summary: Temporary memory or local-file data used by the current work unit that can be discarded or recomputed without violating application correctness.

relations.rationale: Moving persistent correctness state into backing services lets any disposable process serve future work without relying on the previous process's local lifetime.
Statelessness permits temporary process-local working data when its loss is safe and no future request or job depends on it.
